description: The nykur (or nennir) is a water horse from Icelandic folklore, documented by Jón Árnason. It appears as a beautiful grey horse near lakes and rivers, but its hooves are reversed. Anyone who mounts it becomes stuck fast and is dragged into the water to drown. The creature can be defeated by calling its true name, causing it to lose power and vanish.
source: Jón Árnason, Íslenzkar þjóðsögur og ævintýri (1862); snip Simpson, Icelandic Folktales and Legends (1972)
research_notes: Well-attested in Icelandic folklore collections. The 'Glacial Nykur' name is a modern descriptive variant; snip the traditional being is simply the nykur/nennir.

description: The bergsrå (mountain rå) is a Swedish mountain spirit ruling over mines and mineral wealth. It appears as an elderly figure in miner's garb or fine court clothes, sometimes with rocky skin. It can reveal ore deposits to favored humans or cause bergtagning (abduction into the mountain). The 1691 trial of Sven Andersson for intercourse with a bergsrå is a famous historical record.
source: Swedish folk belief; snip Grimberg & snip Åberg, Svenska folkets underbara öden (1960); snip Hultkrantz, The Supernatural Owners of Nature (1961)
research_notes: Well-documented in Swedish ethnographic records and trial documents. The record's 'Bergsrået' is the definite form; snip traditional name is bergsrå.

description: The Bysen is a Gotland-specific forest gnome condemned to wander for moving boundary markers. He carries an axe, appears as a grey little man or a stump, and wears a red cap. He misleads travelers, delays timber transports, and tips loads. Turning one's garment inside out breaks his enchantment. Mainland Sweden has the similar skälvrängare (unholy land-surveyor).
source: Swedish folklore from Gotland; snip Troll Blog archives; snip Deildegast parallels in Norwegian tradition
research_notes: Specific to Gotland island folklore. Well-attested in Swedish regional collections.

description: The bäckahästen (brook horse) is a Swedish manifestation of the näcken water spirit. It appears as a magnificent white or dappled horse near streams and fords. When mounted, it lengthens to accommodate more riders, then dashes into deep water to drown them. It can be controlled by carving a cross on its back or knowing its true name. Closely parallels the Scottish kelpie and Norwegian nøkken.
source: Swedish folk belief; snip Nixie/Näcken tradition across Nordic folklore; snip Kittelsen illustrations
research_notes: Well-attested across Swedish folklore. The record's 'Bäckahästen' is the definite form; snip traditional name is bäckahäst.

description: Not independently attested in Danish tradition as a named being. Danish folklore has generic nature spirits (ellefolk, huldrefolk) and flower-associated beliefs (e.g., elder tree mother), but 'Blomsterfolk' as tiny flower-born guardians appears to be a modern literary invention or conflation. The closest analogue is the general Scandinavian vättar/huldrefolk who inhabit natural features.
source: Danish folk belief surveys; snip no specific 'Blomsterfolk' in Dansk Folkemindesamling collections
research_notes: No historical Danish sources name 'Blomsterfolk' as a distinct entity. Likely a modern neologism. Danish tradition has ellepiger (elf-maidens) and huldre, but not flower-specific tiny guardians.

description: Not independently attested in Nordic tradition as a named hybrid being. Nordic folklore has trolls (trold, jätte) and witches (hejre, klok gumma) as distinct categories; snip 'witch-troll' is a modern descriptive conflation. The closest analogues are trollkonor (troll-wives) who practice magic, or the Finnish hiisi beings blending troll and sorcerer traits.
source: Scandinavian folklore; snip no 'witch-troll' in Nordic folkloric taxonomies (Afzelius, Grundtvig, Árnason)
research_notes: Generic descriptor, not a specific folkloric entity. Trolls and witches are separate categories in all Nordic collections.

description: Refers to Grip, the magical talking bird from the Danish literary fairy tale 'The Bird Grip' (Fuglen Grip), collected by Svend Grundtvig and E.T. Kristensen. Grip aids the hero with guidance and warnings. While talking birds appear in Nordic oral tales (e.g., the raven in Icelandic legends), Grip is specifically a literary fairy-tale figure, not a folkloric being with independent tradition.
source: Grundtvig & snip Kristensen, Danske Folkeæventyr (1876-1901); snip 'The Bird Grip' tale type ATU 550
research_notes: Attested as literary fairy-tale character (Grip), not as independent folkloric spirit. Danish origin, not Swedish as record suggests.

description: Not independently attested as a named 'sea troll' (havstroll) in Nordic folklore. Swedish tradition has sjörå (sea rå) and havsfrun (sea lady) as female water spirits, and the Norwegian havtroll appears in Ibsen's literary Peer Gynt. The generic 'sea troll' is a modern categorization, not a specific folkloric entity.
source: Nordic folklore; snip sjörå/havsfrun tradition; snip Ibsen's Peer Gynt (1867) for literary havtroll
research_notes: No traditional 'sea troll' in Swedish collections. Sjörå is the attested sea spirit; snip 'havstroll' is literary/modern.

description: Not independently attested as a named 'specter' entity in Swedish folklore. Swedish tradition has gäst (ghost of the dead), mårtensgås (harbinger), and vättar, but 'specter' is an English generic term. The record's linked stories (Yuletide specters, Fjelkinge specter) refer to gäster or spöken, not a distinct being type.
source: Swedish ghost lore (gäst, spöke); snip no 'specter' as entity type in folkloric taxonomies
research_notes: English loanword applied generically. Swedish tradition distinguishes gäst (returned dead), spöke (haunting spirit), and vardøger (premonitory double).

description: Not independently attested as a named entity in Nordic folklore. Talking foxes appear in fairy tales (ATU 370 'The Fox as Shepherd') and fables, but not as a recurring folkloric being with a specific name or role. The closest analogue is the fox as trickster in pan-European tales, not a Nordic-specific spirit.
source: Nordic folk tale indexes (ATU); snip no named 'talking fox' being in Swedish/Danish/Icelandic collections
research_notes: Generic fairy-tale motif, not a folkloric entity. Foxes speak in tales but have no independent tradition as a named being.

description: Not independently attested in Swedish folklore. Trolls in Nordic tradition are earth-bound (mountain, forest, sea); snip flight is not a traditional attribute. The 'flying troll' appears in the literary fairy tale 'Dag and Daga and the Flying Troll of Sky Mountain' but this is a modern fairy-tale construction, not oral tradition.
source: Swedish folklore collections (Afzelius, Hyltén-Cavallius); snip no flying trolls in oral tradition
research_notes: Literary invention only. Traditional trolls are tied to specific localities (berg, skog, sjö) and do not fly.

description: The swan maiden (svanejomfru) is a widespread European motif (ATU 400), attested in Danish (Svend Grundtvig), Swedish, and Icelandic collections. A man steals a swan woman's feather cloak, forcing marriage until she recovers it. In Nordic versions, she is often a huldra or elf-woman. The motif is documented but not a specifically 'Swedish' named being.
source: Grundtvig, Danske Folkeæventyr; snip Icelandic variants in Árnason; snip pan-European ATU 400
research_notes: Well-attested motif across Europe, including Nordic regions. Not a single named being but a tale type with regional variants.

description: The magpie (skata) is a bird of Swedish folk belief, regarded as an omen of sorrow or news: its chatter ('skata skriker') and thieving habits were read as signs, and it features in the tale 'The Magpie with Salt on Her Tail' as a clever bird. While not a supernatural being in its own right, it carries genuine omen beliefs in Nordic tradition.
source: Swedish folk belief (omen bird)
research_notes: Bird with folkloric associations, not a supernatural entity. The record treats a common bird as a spirit being.

description: The Trauco is a dwarf-like forest spirit from Chilote mythology (Chiloé Archipelago, Chile). Ugly, footless, and powerfully magnetic, he seduces and impregnates women, who are considered blameless due to his irresistible allure. He carries a stone hatchet to strike trees, symbolizing potency. His wife is the equally hideous Fiura. Child of the snake god Coi Coi-Vilu.
source: Chilote mythology; snip Radio Santiago (2019); snip Roth, American Elves (1997); snip Rebolledo Muller (2012)
research_notes: Well-documented in Chilote oral tradition and ethnographic literature. Specific to Chiloé.

description: Not independently attested in Chilote or Chilean tradition as a distinct 'fire variant' of the Trauco. The Trauco is a single entity; snip regional variants or 'fire forms' are not documented in primary sources. This appears to be a modern elaboration or RPG-style elemental variant with no folkloric basis.
source: Chilean mythology collections; snip no 'Trauco del Fuego' in Chilote ethnography (Cárdenas, Guevara, Larraín)
research_notes: Fabricated elemental variant. Chilote tradition has one Trauco; snip no fire/ice/earth subtypes in sources.

description: Trentren Vilu is the benevolent land serpent in the Mapuche flood myth, opponent of Caicai Vilu. He raises hills to save humans and animals from Caicai's flood, transforms the trapped into birds and fish, and becomes the mountain ranges walling the valley. Associated with earthquakes and volcanic eruptions. Documented by Faron (1963), Bastías et al. (2021), and Mapuche oral tradition.
source: Mapuche mythology; snip Faron, 'The Magic Mountain' (1963); snip Bastías et al., Earth Sciences History (2021)
research_notes: Core Mapuche cosmological figure. Well-documented in ethnographic and geological literature.

description: Tsunki is the primordial water spirit of the Shuar and Achuar (Jivaroan peoples, Ecuador/Peru). Appears as a beautiful woman or anaconda near remote waterfalls. Source of all shamanic power (tsentsak); snip grants crystal tsentsak to initiates. Features in myths 'The Tsunki and the Hunter' and 'Tsunki and the Chased Woman'. Documented by Perruchon (2003), Whitten (2008), Beyer (2009).
source: Shuar/Achuar ethnography; snip Perruchon, I Am Tsunki (2003); snip Beyer, Singing to the Plants (2009); snip Whitten, Puyo Runa (2008)
research_notes: Well-documented in Jivaroan shamanic tradition. Central to Shuar cosmology and shamanic initiation.

description: La Tunda is an Afro-Colombian/Afro-Ecuadorian shapeshifting spirit from the Pacific coastal region (Chocó, Esmeraldas). She mimics loved ones to lure victims into the forest, feeding them shrimp to induce entundamiento (docile stupor). Her disguise is flawed: she always has a wooden leg shaped like a molinillo (chocolate whisk).
source: González Cortés, Fantasmagorías (2001); snip Puertas Arias, La Tunda: Mito y realidad (2000); snip Colombian/Ecuadorian Pacific oral tradition
research_notes: Well-attested in Afro-Colombian and Afro-Ecuadorian Pacific coastal tradition. Distinct from indigenous Amazonian beings.

description: Not independently attested in Quechua tradition as a named 'turtle animal-spirit guardian of swamps'. Andean cosmology includes animal spirits (apus, wak'as) but no specific turtle guardian of swamps is documented in ethnographic literature (Métraux, Urton, Salomon). The turtle appears in some origin myths but not as a distinct named entity with this role.
source: Andean ethnography (Métraux, Urton, Salomon); snip no turtle swamp guardian in Quechua sources
research_notes: Fabricated entry. Quechua tradition has mountain apus and animal alter-egos, but no named turtle swamp guardian.

description: Not independently attested in Muisca tradition as a named 'turtle nature-spirit guardian of swamps'. Muisca cosmology (Bochica, Chía, Sué) centers on solar/lunar deities and culture heroes; snip animal spirits are not prominently documented as named guardians. The turtle appears in some Chibcha art but not as a distinct spirit entity with this title.
source: Muisca/Chibcha ethnography (Simón, Ocampo López, Langebaek); snip no turtle nature-spirit in primary sources
research_notes: Fabricated entry. Muisca tradition lacks named animal-spirit guardians of this type.

description: Not independently attested in Aymara tradition as a named 'turtle trickster guardian of rivers'. Aymara mythology features the trickster fox (Zorro) and culture heroes (Thunupa, Tunupa), but no turtle trickster is documented in Métraux, Bouysse-Cassagne, or Plata ethnography. Turtles are not prominent in high-altitude Altiplano mythology.
source: Aymara ethnography (Métraux, Bouysse-Cassagne, Plata); snip no turtle trickster in Aymara sources
research_notes: Fabricated entry. Aymara trickster is the fox; snip turtles are ecologically marginal in Altiplano.

description: Not independently attested in Muisca tradition as a named 'turtle water-spirit guardian of hills'. Muisca water deities center on Bochica (culture hero who drained floods) and the lake goddess Sie; snip no turtle water-spirit is documented. This appears to be a generic template entry with no basis in Chibcha ethnography.
source: Muisca/Chibcha ethnography (Simón, Ocampo López); snip no turtle water-spirit in primary sources
research_notes: Fabricated template entry. Muisca water mythology focuses on Bochica and lake deities, not turtle spirits.

description: The Tunche is a fearsome whistling spirit of the Peruvian Amazon (Shipibo-Conibo, Asháninka traditions). It mimics bird calls and human voices to lure travelers off paths at night. Its whistle signals approaching death. Described as a shadowy, faceless entity or a glowing presence. Fearlessness and spiritual protection (tobacco, ayahuasca) can ward it off.
source: Peruvian Amazonian ethnography; snip Shipibo-Conibo oral tradition; snip urban Lima folklore collections
research_notes: Well-attested in Peruvian Amazonian traditions and modern urban folklore. The 'whistling spirit' motif is widespread.

description: Amaru (or katari in Aymara) is the cosmic serpent/dragon of Andean mythology (Inca, pre-Inca). A double-headed serpent dwelling in lakes and rivers, connecting the earthly world (kay pacha) with the underworld (uku pacha) and upper world (hanan pacha). Represents infinity, wisdom, water, lightning, and the Milky Way.
source: Steele, Handbook of Inca Mythology (2004); snip Bauer, American Anthropologist (1996); snip Smith, Ancient America (2011); snip Tiwanaku iconography
research_notes: Core Andean cosmological figure. Well-documented in archaeology, ethnohistory, and Quechua/Aymara oral tradition.

description: Madremonte (Madre Monte, 'Mother of the Mountain') is a Colombian nature spirit protecting wilderness, especially in Andean and Pacific regions. Punishes deforestation, pollution, and harm to nature. Appears as a large woman covered in moss and leaves, with glowing eyes. Blend of Muisca earth goddess traditions and Spanish Catholic influences (Virgin Mary syncretism).
source: Colombian folklore collections; snip Ministerio de Cultura Colombia; snip Muisca-Spanish syncretism studies
research_notes: Well-attested in Colombian oral tradition across regions. Living tradition with environmental significance.

description: Mama Qucha (Mama Cocha, 'Mother Sea/Lake') is the Inca goddess of the sea, lakes, and all waters. Wife of Wiraqucha, mother of Inti (Sun) and Mama Killa (Moon). One of four Elemental Mothers with Pachamama, Mama Nina, Mama Wayra. Worshipped by coastal peoples for calm seas and good fishing; snip inland peoples honored her as lake goddess. Inhabits Hanan Pacha (upper world).
source: Inca mythology; snip Roza, Incan Mythology (2008); snip Issitt & snip Main, Hidden Religion (2014); snip Quechua lexicon (Martínez Compañón)
research_notes: Major Inca deity. Well-documented in chronicles (Cieza de León, Garcilaso) and Quechua tradition.

description: Manco Cápac (Manqu Qhapaq) is the legendary founder and first Sapa Inca of Cusco (c. 1200 CE). In the Ayar brothers legend, he emerges from Paqariq Tampu with a golden staff, disposes of his brothers, and founds Cusco. In the Inti legend, he is the son of Sun god Inti and Moon goddess Mama Killa, sent from Lake Titicaca to bring civilization.
source: Cieza de León; snip Garcilaso de la Vega, Comentarios Reales (1609); snip Guaman Poma; snip Prescott, Conquest of Peru; snip Covey, Comparative Studies (2006)
research_notes: Central Inca culture hero. Documented in multiple chronicles and oral traditions. Not a 'water spirit' as record mislabels.

description: The Mapinguari is a giant hairy cryptid of Brazilian Amazon folklore (Tupi-Guarani mbaé-pi-guari: 'thing with twisted feet'). Described as monkey-like, bipedal, with backwards feet, a single eye (forehead or belly), a vertical mouth from nose to stomach, and foul odor. Bulletproof except at navel. Devours human heads. Linked to extinct ground sloth (Glossotherium) folk memory by Oren (1993).
source: Cascudo, Dicionário do Folclore Brasileiro (1962/1983); snip Oren, Goeldi Museum (1993); snip Shepard, Primates Face to Face (2002); snip NYT Rohter (2007)
research_notes: Major Amazonian cryptid. Well-documented in Brazilian folklore, cryptozoology, and ethnographic literature.

description: Mboreví (Mborevi) are miniature forest-dwelling nature spirits in Guaraní tradition (Paraguay, NE Argentina, S Brazil). Described as small protective people who guard the forest and its creatures. They punish those who harm nature and can be appeased with offerings. Closely related to Pombero and Kurupi in the Guaraní spirit complex. Documented by Cadogan and Guaraní ethnographers.
source: Guaraní folklore; snip Cadogan, Chonó Kvbwirá (1968); snip regional oral tradition in Paraguay/Argentina/Brazil
research_notes: Attested in Guaraní tradition but less documented than Pombero/Kurupi. Part of the forest spirit complex.

description: Momoy are small, bearded duende-like guardians of water sources, rivers, forests, and agricultural lands in Venezuelan Andean folklore (Mérida, Táchira, Trujillo). Mischievous but protective; snip can summon heavy rains. Leave offerings to gain favor. Blend of indigenous Timoto-Cuica beliefs and Spanish duende traditions. Documented in Venezuelan regional folklore collections.
source: Venezuelan Andean folklore; snip regional collections (Mérida/Táchira); snip Timoto-Cuica syncretism
research_notes: Regional Venezuelan Andean tradition. Less documented nationally but attested in local collections.

description: This entry conflates Kurupi with a moon deity. Kurupi is a Guaraní forest spirit, one of seven monstrous children of Tau and Kerana, known for his elongated prehensile phallus, backwards feet, and role as abductor/impregnator of women. He is a fertility figure and forest guardian, not a moon god.
source: Guaraní mythology; snip Cadogan (1968); snip Carvalho Neto (1992); snip Blache (1977); snip Perruchon (2003) for Kurupi; snip no moon god named Kurupi
research_notes: Misattribution: entry describes Kurupi (attested) but labels it 'Moon God' (false). Kurupi is forest/fertility spirit, not lunar deity.

description: Not independently attested in Mapuche tradition. Moose (Alces alces) are native to North America and Eurasia, NOT South America. The Mapuche have no moose in their mythology. Their guardians include the Ngen (spirit owners of nature), Pillán (volcano spirits), and animal spirits like the fox (Zorro) or puma.
source: Mapuche ethnography (Métraux, Faron, Bacigalupo, González); snip no moose in South American fauna or mythology
research_notes: Fabricated: moose do not exist in South America. Mapuche guardians are Ngen, Pillán, and local fauna spirits (puma, fox, condor).

description: Not independently attested in Aymara tradition. Moose are absent from South America. Aymara high-altitude mythology (Altiplano) features camelids (llama, vicuña), condors, and fox tricksters, not moose. Lake guardians include the serpent Amaru and mountain deities (Achachila). 'Moose Guardian' is a fabricated template entry.
source: Aymara ethnography (Métraux, Bouysse-Cassagne, Plata); snip no moose in Andean fauna or mythology
research_notes: Fabricated: moose do not exist in South America. Aymara lake/mountain spirits are Amaru, Achachila, and camelid deities.

description: Not independently attested in Mapuche tradition. Duplicate of mooseguardianmapuche-chile with different habitat description ('undergrounds'). Moose are not native to South America. Mapuche underground spirits are the Ngen-mapu (earth owners) and Anchimayen (little people), not moose guardians.
source: Mapuche ethnography (Métraux, Bacigalupo); snip no moose in South American fauna or Mapuche mythology
research_notes: Duplicate fabricated entry. Same error: moose absent from South America.

description: Not independently attested in Muisca tradition. Moose are absent from South America. Muisca mythology (Bacatá/ Bogotá savanna) centers on Bochica, Chía, Sué, and lake deities (Sie). No cervid guardians of cliffs exist; snip the spectacled bear (oso de anteojos) is the largest native mammal. 'Moose Guardian' is a fabricated template entry.
source: Muisca/Chibcha ethnography (Simón, Ocampo López, Langebaek); snip no moose in Colombian fauna or mythology
research_notes: Fabricated: moose do not exist in South America. Muisca cliff/mountain spirits are Bochica-related, not cervid guardians.
